item.title: Operation ASTERIX: Anatomy of a Crypto Fraud Pipeline
item.description:
Operation ASTERIX: AI-assisted crypto fraud pipeline combines bulk phone validation, coordinated phishing and vishing, and counterfeit Trezor, Ledger, and Exodus apps to steal BIP39 seed phrases via Telegram exfiltration.
- Attackers validated ~885,000 phone numbers across 54 countries against Crypto.com and Kraken APIs using 300 concurrent threads and rotating Bright Data proxies (T1589.002). A German 🇩🇪 dataset returned 13.6% confirmed accounts. Enriched lead records with names, emails, and exchange details were then used to make vishing calls sound like legitimate support contacts.
- The fake Trezor Suite (app.asar SHA-256 ba9d459169a303067a4fe36c8b8582a5ea023b9c270dafe89613bab840501b19) ran as a hidden 1x1 pixel Electron window, killed the real Trezor process via kill -9, and swapped in its phishing UI (T1185, T1564.003). Stolen phrases were exfiltrated to Telegram prefixed with "TREZOR SECRET PHRASE" (T1567). Persistence via LaunchAgents com.trezormovement.agent.plist and io.trezor.agent.plist.
- A trojanized Claude Code installer at macos-claude[.]com silently dropped fake Ledger Live into ~/Library/Application Support/.SystemData/.framework/.apps/ and hid the directory with chflags hidden. The Ledger Windows build included a clipboard hijacker replacing crypto addresses (T1115).
- The operator used Claude Code and GitHub Copilot throughout development.

item.title: From CI Pipeline to Ransomware & Breaches: 6 High-Profile Breaches in the LiteLLM/Trivy Attack
item.description:
A poisoned LiteLLM/Trivy supply chain attack hit 250+ enterprises via CI/CD pipelines, exposing AWS keys, GitHub PATs, and RSA private keys that fueled ransomware extortion by the Vect group (TeamPCP).
Key findings:
- The attack harvested secrets directly from CI runner environment dumps: AWS STS session tokens, long-lived IAM keys, GitHub PATs, JWTs, RSA private keys, Artifactory tokens, Conjur API keys, and Docker configs with base64-encoded credentials. Secrets were logged in plain text inside pipeline logs, making exfiltration trivial once a poisoned container executed.
- Six named victims illustrate the blast radius: Guesty (700GB, 4M emails, AWS/Kubernetes secrets), S&P Global (250GB, thousands of secrets from terraform-actions workflows), Cisco (source code via scraped GitHub PATs and a Conjur API key), the European Commission (AWS IAM creds plus a hardcoded SSH key and GitLab CI tokens), Mercor (4TB including 939GB source code and SSNs/biometrics of 40,000+ contractors), and Telnyx (malicious PyPI SDK versions 4.87.1 and 4.87.2 published March 27, 2026).
- Lapsus$ claimed to have sold Mercor's biometric, PII, and AI training data to Chinese 🇨🇳 enterprises. Meta paused a data contract and class-action lawsuits followed.
- On the detection side: look for unexpected child processes spawned by CI runner agents, outbound connections from runner hosts to unfamiliar endpoints, and any secrets appearing in raw job logs stored in your artifact repository.

item.title: Akira Ransomware Uses Safe Mode to Bypass EDR
item.description:
Akira ransomware affiliate used Safe Mode to kill EDR before encrypting, but the stripped-down memory environment crashed the encryptor. Data was already exfiltrated, so the victim faces extortion regardless.
- Initial access via MFA-less SonicWall VPN at 03:52 UTC on August 4. Two hours of quiet followed before the operator RDP'd to the domain controller, dumped all AD users and group memberships via PowerShell with truncation disabled, archived file shares with WinRAR, and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket using s5cmd. Encryption came last, meaning failed ransomware does not mean no harm.
- The Safe Mode pivot is new for Akira in Huntress telemetry. The affiliate added AnyDesk to the Safe Mode service registry before rebooting, preserving remote access through the restart (T1562.001). EDR and Defender real-time protection were both down for roughly ten minutes.
- akira.exe launched at 06:34:29 UTC, spawned its child-process burst at 06:36:21, and hit out-of-virtual-memory failures about 13 seconds later. Defender eventually flagged it as Ransom:Win32/Akira.B!ibt but could not quarantine in Safe Mode. Rebooting to normal mode restored Defender, which then removed the file automatically.
Hunt for bcdedit or msconfig.exe activity, Kernel-Boot Event ID 27 with SAFEBOOT option, Kernel-General Event ID 12 with BootMode=2, and third-party services stopping abruptly.

item.title: Three NTFS bugs, one VHD file, and what your logs should already be telling you
item.description:
Three NTFS heap overflows in ntfs.sys, all triggerable via a single malicious VHD file, patched July 2026 across roughly 30 Windows client and server editions. No public PoC confirmed yet, but the forensic window before patching deserves scrutiny.
- CVE-2026-50471 (CVSS 7.8), CVE-2026-50494 (CVSS 7.8), and CVE-2026-58640 (CVSS 7.3) all share the same CWE-122 root cause: ntfs.sys allocates a heap buffer using one size, writes using a mismatched length, corrupting adjacent kernel pool memory. CVE-2026-50494 is the most dangerous operationally as it requires only local low-privilege access with no user interaction to escalate to SYSTEM. The other two need a user to open the file, a trivial social engineering bar given VHD has no "are you sure" prompt on double-click since Windows 8.
- The delivery chain is deliberately low-friction. Windows Explorer auto-mounts a VHD like a ZIP archive. Attackers can deliver it via email, chat, or cloud link with a plausible backup or disk image cover story. APT-C-60 already used VHDX as an attack vector in a documented campaign analyzed by Positive Technologies.
- NTFS itself logs the attack. The USN Journal ($Extend\$UsnJrnl) retains create, rename, and delete events for roughly 20 days even after the VHD is removed. The $LogFile records low-level metadata transactions that can show heap corruption fingerprints even without a system crash.

item.title: APT36 Suspected in PATCHCORD Espionage Campaign Using Google Sheets C2
item.description:
APT36 suspected in PATCHCORD espionage campaign targeting Afghan telecom and South Asian critical infrastructure using Google Sheets and GitHub Gists for C2.
- PATCHCORD is a compiled C/C++ backdoor delivered via fake VPN installers impersonating Afghan Telecom (AFTEL) and telecom management tools. Persistence is established by hijacking browser shortcuts for Edge, Chrome, and Firefox: originals are backed up, shortcuts rewritten to silently launch the implant first, then the real browser, so the victim notices nothing. Five core capabilities include in-memory shellcode execution (payload never touches disk), remote shell, process listing, beacon interval control, and remote persistence management.
- SHEETCORD, a Go-based evolution of the toolset, uses the Google Sheets API for C2, creating a per-victim spreadsheet tab to send and receive commands. It was distributed via a domain impersonating India 🇮🇳's National Informatics Centre. A third implant, HACKERAI C2 Agent, uses GitHub Gists for C2 and shows signs of LLM-assisted development.
- An exposed staging server revealed the operator's full toolkit: SuperShell C2 framework (Chinese-language), multiple RAT frameworks, credential-harvesting tools, OpenSSH exploit code, and files resembling iOS call history databases, suggesting mobile data collection as well.

item.title: Plist Files: Structure, Forensic Value, and How to Analyze Them
item.description:
Plist files are everywhere in Apple investigations: Wi-Fi history, Bluetooth pairings, app state, device identity. Knowing how to read them correctly is not optional for macOS and iOS casework.
Key findings:
- Binary plist (bplist) is the default format since Mac OS X 10.2. It opens with the signature bplist00 and is parsed backward: trailer first (last 32 bytes), then offset table, then root object. The trailer supplies offset integer size, object reference size, object count, root object index, and offset table location. Every other read depends on those values. A parser that hardcodes root object index 0 will silently decode the wrong subtree when the root is elsewhere.
- Dates are stored relative to the Cocoa epoch (January 1, 2001, 00:00:00 UTC), not the Unix epoch. Applying the wrong reference point shifts every timestamp by 31 years. Verify before you report.
- NSKeyedArchiver files embed an object graph using UID references rather than flat key-value pairs. Spotting UID entries in a plist is your signal that you are not looking at a simple settings file. Walking those references by hand is slow and error-prone; the parser must resolve them for you.
- High-value iOS plist paths: com.apple.wifi.known-networks.plist (SSID, BSSID, join timestamps, iOS 16+), com.apple.Bluetooth.plist (paired device names, hardware addresses, pairing timestamps), data_ark.plist (device name, time zone, phone number), and pair_records (trusted host identifiers).

item.title: The LiteLLM Supply-Chain Attack — TeamPCP “SANDCLOCK” CI/CD Credential-Harvesting Campaign via a Backdoored Trivy GitHub Action
item.description:
TeamPCP "SANDCLOCK" backdoored the Trivy GitHub Action in March 2026, harvesting 415,427 CI secret dumps from 898 orgs including Microsoft, NVIDIA, IBM, and PayPal across a chained supply-chain attack that poisoned LiteLLM on PyPI.
Key findings:
- The attack chain ran Trivy to LiteLLM: TeamPCP compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action on 19 Mar 2026 (T1195.001), victim CI pipelines auto-installed it, SANDCLOCK escalated to root, read /proc/pid/mem and process env, then published malicious litellm==1.82.7/1.82.8 to PyPI on 24 Mar. Capture files follow the naming pattern YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_us_127.0.0.1.txt with records structured as "name":{"value":"secret","isSecret":true}.
- The 152.5 GiB archive holds 415,427 per-run secret dumps across 2,038 repos. GITHUB_TOKEN (system.github.token) appeared in ~98% of sampled files. Alongside it: GitHub App private keys, AWS/GovCloud ECR tokens, GCP service accounts, JFrog JWTs, SSH keys, and signing passwords. Persistent secrets do not expire with the ephemeral token.
- Named victims in the owners manifest include Microsoft, Azure, IBM, NVIDIA, FedEx, John Deere, Deloitte, S&P Global, ID.me, Dräger, and a US 🇺🇸 GovCloud AWS ECR tenant (071032557399.dkr.ecr.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws[.]com), raising national-security sensitivity.

item.title: MAJINAHANASHI RANSOMWARE: Yet Another Japanese Locker
item.description:
MAJINAHANASHI ransomware emerges August 2026 targeting US 🇺🇸, Swiss 🇨🇭, and EU orgs with double extortion. C/C++ locker drops .MAJIN-encrypted files, kills EDR tooling, and uses WFP to silence agent comms.
- Two 90KB C/C++ samples (SHA-256: bd91d786841f5259430c1c90b454d9f8bf510186fe4d32a0998bd9b5a7916467 and e6ec7749e3d0f750fa53b5a7619d1e5af57673d236338b3a020d0f534ec5c15d) created July 2, 2026. AES-256 per-file encryption with RSA-wrapped keys; marker string ENCRYPTEDAES256!SCT2 written to encrypted files. Mutex Global\majinahanashi_Mutex and service majinSvc register persistence. Drop paths: C:\Windows\Temp\majin.exe and ADMIN$\Temp\majin.exe for lateral movement via admin shares.
- Pre-flight kills Carbon Black, CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Veeam, Acronis, and others before encrypting. Deletes VSS (vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet), clears event logs (wevtutil), wipes USN journal (fsutil usn deletejournal), and disables recovery via bcdedit. WFP filters named majinahanashi WFP network control and qos_silence actively interfere with EDR and cloud agent callbacks, an uncommon technique worth flagging.
- Wallpaper hijacked via dual registry write: HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, making user-level cleanup insufficient.

item.title: Revisiting JWT Token Forgery Attack on Recent Bounty Target
item.description:
A partner portal accepted unsigned JWTs with alg=none, letting an unauthenticated researcher enumerate the full partner directory, including billing data and contact records, with no valid account or session.
Key findings:
- The API validated that token.partner_id matched the query string id param, but both values came from the forged token itself. The "authorization check" existed and was enforced, yet it compared two attacker-controlled values against each other, making it meaningless (MITRE T1550.001 adjacent abuse of auth tokens).
- Exploitation was a simple loop: craft a none-algorithm JWT with sub and partners.id set to the target pid, append the required trailing dot for an empty third segment, send GET /api/partner?id={pid}. Records returned account numbers, billing methods, addresses, and company emails with zero rate limiting observed.
- The researcher confirmed specificity by testing five token variants: no token returned 500, malformed tokens were rejected, RS256 with a real signature was rejected, HS256 with a tampered signature was rejected. Only alg=none succeeded, ruling out accidental data leakage.
- The article also catalogs the broader JWT attack family worth testing: alg case variations (None, NONE, nOnE), signature stripping, RS256-to-HS256 confusion using the public key as HMAC secret, jwk/jku/x5u header injection, kid path traversal to /dev/null, kid SQL/command injection, and cross-environment key reuse via JWKS modulus comparison.

item.title: Escalating a Blind Upload to RCE via Path Traversal into Cron and DNS-Restricted Callback Bypass
item.description:
Unauthenticated blind file upload escalated to root RCE via path traversal into /etc/cron.d, bypassing forced UUID/.png renaming entirely. CVSS 3.1 score: 10.0 Critical.
Key findings:
- The endpoint at /app/api/files/upload required zero authentication and passed the uploadPath field directly into a filesystem write with no sanitization, allowing 14-segment traversal (../../../../../../../../../../../../../../etc/cron.d) to escape the upload root and land files anywhere the process could write. Absolute paths, encoded separators, and relative components were all accepted.
- The backend ran as root, confirmed via a blind filesystem oracle: writing to /proc failed (kernel blocks arbitrary directory creation there) while /root and /etc succeeded. This write-only oracle answered yes/no questions about filesystem state by distinguishing directory-creation errors from success responses, enabling host fingerprinting (RHEL/CentOS, crond present, no .dockerenv).
- Cron processed the UUID-named .png as a valid system crontab because it reads directory contents by file content, not extension. A self-removing crontab planted in /etc/cron.d executed as root one cycle later, confirmed by the oracle detecting /tmp/bugbounty-cronproof.
- DNS egress was blocked, but curl --resolve mapped a controlled hostname directly to an attacker IP, bypassing the resolver entirely. The callback returned uid=0(root) gid=0(root) context=system_u:system_r:system_cronjob_t.

item.title: Stealing the Artifact – JFrog Artifactory Vulnerability
item.description:
Two chained CVEs in JFrog Artifactory let an unauthenticated attacker bypass auth, traverse paths, and exfiltrate arbitrary artifacts. All OSS and Enterprise versions below the patched releases were affected.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-42018 (auth bypass): POSTing to /access/api/v1/aws/token/ with a trailing slash causes AntPathMatcher to skip AwsTokenAuthenticationFilter entirely. Spring's fallback AnonymousAuthenticationFilter then populates the security context, and the AWS token endpoint mints a valid JWT for the anonymous user, even when anonymous access is disabled. Patch: Artifactory 7.146.8.
- CVE-2026-69107 (missing authz + path traversal): The JWT unlocks the deprecated stash API. An attacker POSTs arbitrary repoKey and relativePath values; FileInfo (sha1, sha256, size) is loaded into the session with no ACL check. The stash export then concatenates an attacker-controlled name containing ../ sequences with a base directory, and forceMkdir resolves the traversal, dropping the artifact into the Tomcat web root.
- Bug 4 completes the production chain: jf-router does not normalize paths before proxying, so /artifactory/..;/markertag-20260713.141536/sample-v1.0.0 routes through Traefik to Tomcat, which strips the path parameter and serves the file unauthenticated.
- The stash oracle is a bonus primitive: a 200 vs error response confirms whether a repo name and artifact path exist, enabling blind enumeration before full exfiltration.

item.title: LiteLLM Supply Chain Attack: Inside the AI Breach That Exposed 2,500+ Companies
item.description:

Row-level timestamps show 95% of the 2,188 organizations in the dataset had collection activity before March 24, with the earliest record at 18:05 UTC on March 19, eighteen minutes after the malicious Trivy build.
- Execution required no import. Version 1.82.8 shipped litellm_init.pth, a Python startup file that ran the SANDCLOCK stealer at interpreter start regardless of whether any code imported LiteLLM. The payload escalated to root, swept SSH keys, AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS tokens, .kube/config, .env secrets, OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and GitHub Actions masked variables from /proc/pid/mem. item.title: ARM64 stack internals and obfuscation on Apple Silicon
item.description:
ARM64 call-stack spoofing lands on Apple Silicon: MDSec reverse-engineers how to build synthetic frame chains that fool macOS EDR sensors relying on spindump for thread-stack collection.
- A major EDR vendor delegates call-stack collection to /usr/sbin/spindump, macOS's own diagnostic tool. That design choice becomes exploitable: spindump trusts the frame-pointer chain anchored at x29 and return addresses stored at [x29+0x8], walking the linked list without verifying whether frames were built by a real prologue or constructed in memory.
- Synthetic frames work by reversing the unwinder's logic. Pick real executable PCs that have valid __TEXT,__unwind_info entries (compact-unwind mode 0x04000000 FRAME or 0x02000000 FRAMELESS), allocate matching memory at the required x29-relative offsets, then set live x29 and x30 so the unwinder walks the fake chain instead of the real call history.
- On ARM64e Apple Silicon, every saved LR is PAC-signed with key B and the frame's entry SP as discriminator: signedLR = PACIB(rawPC, CFA) where CFA = FP + 0x10. Synthetic frames must replicate this per-frame signing or authentication fails. A trampoline gadget frame, a branch-to-register inside a dylib cache image, bridges the fake chain back to implant code in unbacked memory.
- The DFIR impact: EDR call-stack telemetry on macOS can be fed a fabricated call history (dyld_start, then benign-looking framework symbols, then the target API), hiding the true origin.

item.title: Digital Forensics: AnyDesk – Favorite Tool of APTs
item.description:
AnyDesk artifact guide: four log files that expose remote attacker sessions, connecting IPs, display names, OS fingerprints, and file transfer activity during IR.
Key findings:
- Four priority log paths: C:\Users\%username%\AppData\Roaming\AnyDesk\ad.trace, connection_trace.txt (portable installs), and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk\ad_svc.trace, connection_trace.txt (service installs). The service-mode ad_svc.trace is the richest artifact, containing "Logged in from" with the attacker's external IP and "Accepting from" with their AnyDesk ID.
- Grep ad.trace for "Incoming session request" to recover the attacker's display name and AnyDesk ID. One documented case showed a Linux machine connecting with the alias "IT Dep" to appear legitimate. Remote OS field also surfaces in these logs.
- File transfer activity appears in ad.trace as "Preparing files in ..." entries. Correlate those timestamps with Windows artifacts (Prefetch, MFT, Shellbags) to reconstruct exactly what was staged or exfiltrated.
- Threat context: Crypt Ghouls (Q4 2024 ICS-CERT) paired AnyDesk with Mimikatz and PsExec. BlackJack (Q3 2024) chained AnyDesk, Radmin, PuTTY, and ngrok across Russian 🇷🇺 government and ICS networks. Both groups used it for durable, low-noise persistence.
Ingest all four paths into your SIEM and alert on AnyDesk connections outside business hours. PowerShell one-liner for triage: get-content ad.trace | select-string 'Remote OS','Incoming session','files','anynet.relay'.

item.title: APT group HoneyMyte upgrades CoolClient: the backdoor gets a kernel-level Windows rootkit
item.description:
HoneyMyte (Mustang Panda) upgrades CoolClient backdoor with a signed kernel-mode rootkit, targeting government entities in Myanmar 🇲🇲, Mongolia 🇲🇳, Pakistan 🇵🇰, and Russia 🇷🇺.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: PlugX lands first as the foothold, then drops CoolClient via DLL sideloading. A legitimate Sangfor binary (renamed defender.exe) loads malicious libngs.dll, which decrypts and injects through loadcert.ini into synchost.exe. Persistence runs via a scheduled task named "\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service" plus an AutoRun key (HKCU\...\Run, value: goopdate), and a service named media_updaten. item.title: Return of the Cookie Monster
item.description:

item.title: Attack of The Extensions
item.description:
SilentChrome-BOF and the Ditto Mythic agent turn Chromium itself into a persistent C2 by silently sideloading extensions, Isolated Web Apps, and Native Messaging Hosts via Secure Preferences tampering.
Key details:
- SilentChrome-BOF (a Cobalt Strike BOF) bypasses Chromium's HMAC integrity checks by recalculating protection.macs and protection.super_mac using the user's SID as part of the HMAC seed, then drops the entire settings_encrypted_hash dictionary so Chromium self-heals on next launch. Targets: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Secure Preferences and the Edge equivalent.
- Ditto is the Mythic agent delivered as an unpacked Chrome extension. It checks in over HTTP(S), collects cookies, enumerates tabs, and captures history. Optional sidecars: a Rust Native Messaging Host (process listing, file ops, COFF execution via HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts) and a signed IWA for Direct Sockets SOCKS pivoting.
- Allowlist bypass: reusing the Base64 public key from a legitimate extension's CRX gives Ditto the same 32-character extension ID, impersonating an enterprise-approved extension.
- Detection anchors: Sysmon Event ID 11 for non-browser writes to \User Data\Secure Preferences; Event IDs 12/13 for HKCU\SOFTWARE*\NativeMessagingHosts* creation; Event ID 1 for chrome.exe or msedge.exe spawning child processes via \\.\pipe\chrome.nativeMessaging pipes; process args containing --enable-isolated-web-apps-in-renderer or --app-id.

item.title: "City-Forum" data-theft attacks target Salesforce, ServiceNow portals
item.description:
Ongoing "City-Forum" campaign systematically harvests data from misconfigured Salesforce Experience Cloud and ServiceNow portals, targeting telecoms, banks, and public-sector orgs worldwide with no vulnerability required.
- Single attacker IP 158.220.87[.]79 (Contabo VPS, Germany 🇩🇪), associated with city-forum[.]com since at least March 2025, hits both platforms using the default Go-http-client/1.1 user agent. One organization logged over 560,000 events from this IP alone. The fingerprint is consistent across every observed intrusion.
- On Salesforce, the attacker enumerates guest-accessible objects via /aura and /s/sfsites/aura endpoints (invoking HostConfigController.getConfigData, then SelectableListDataProviderController.getItems). Notably, they also abuse the newer LWR GraphQL endpoint at /webruntime/api/services/data/{version}/graphql, a technique not seen in public tooling like AuraInspector, S-RET, or CirrusGo.
- On ServiceNow, POST requests to /api/now/sp/search?sysparm_cancelable=true enumerate exposed search sources anonymously. Critical gap: ServiceNow transaction logs omit the POST body, so defenders can see volume and data returned but not the exact search terms used.
Takeaway: Hunt your Salesforce and ServiceNow logs for requests from 158.220.87[.]45 and user-agent Go-http-client/1.1. Audit guest-user sharing rules, object permissions, and self-registration endpoints now.

item.title: Kimwolf v7 Hides DDoS Traffic Behind Chrome Fingerprints and Ethereum
item.description:
Kimwolf v7 Android TV botnet adds Chrome-fingerprinted HTTP/2 floods and Ethereum ENS C2 resolution, making attack traffic and infrastructure harder to block than any prior version.
Key details:
- C2 resilience is now three-tier: Ethereum ENS queried across five shuffled public RPC endpoints (including a suspected operator facade at eth.rpcuniverse[.]com), then a Tor .onion backup, then a local proxy on 127.0.0.1:23075. All three were added directly in response to December 2025 takedowns. Blocking any single RPC node is ineffective.
- The new HTTP/2 flood uses the nghttp2 library to construct full Chrome browser fingerprints at the protocol and header level, defeating fingerprint-based DDoS mitigations. A UDP flood with ARM NEON SIMD acceleration targets the specific processors in Android TV hardware.
- Initial access abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) on port 5555, tunneled through residential proxy services, no authentication required. The bot masquerades as "netd_service" and eight APKs disguised as "SystemService" probed for root between October and December 2025.
- Scale is significant: roughly 1.8 million infected devices, 1.7 billion DDoS commands issued in three days, and a linked 31.4 Tbps peak attack in November 2025. Unit 42 clustered 22 C2 IPs in Saint Petersburg sharing one SSH host key.

item.title: Largest AI Supply Chain Breach of 2026: LiteLLM Hack Impacts Thousands of Global Enterprises – Claim Your Ethical Disclosure
item.description:
TeamPCP's AI supply chain attack hit LiteLLM via a poisoned Trivy CI/CD pipeline, silently exfiltrating secrets from 2,488 enterprises. A 153GB raw dump confirms AWS, Cisco, Samsung, Siemens, and Boeing among victims.
- TeamPCP first compromised the GitHub Actions pipeline for Trivy, a popular open-source vulnerability scanner. Because LiteLLM used Trivy in its own CI/CD pipeline, attackers inherited legitimate runner access and stole LiteLLM's PyPI publishing tokens, then pushed malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8.
- Payload delivery used a .pth Python startup hook, executing the moment the Python interpreter initialized regardless of whether LiteLLM was imported. The three-stage payload harvested environment variables, .kube/config, .aws/credentials, attempted Kubernetes lateral movement, and installed a persistent systemd backdoor masquerading as "System Telemetry Service."
- Hudson Rock obtained the raw 153GB RAR archive: 433,909 files, 118,829 CI runner dumps attributed to 2,488 corporate domains. Exposed secrets include AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET, SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, Azure tokens, and AI provider API keys, many in plain text.
Inspect site-packages directories for unauthorized .pth files and audit systemd services for masquerading entries. Rotate all cloud IAM keys, Kubernetes tokens, and VCS PATs that touched any LiteLLM environment. Review AWS CloudTrail and Kubernetes API audit logs from March 24, 2026 onward.

item.title: Lazarus Used Post-Quantum Key Exchange to Deliver Zero-Day
item.description:
North Korea 🇰🇵's Lazarus group deployed a Windows kernel zero-day via a post-quantum encrypted channel against defense and aerospace firms in France 🇫🇷, Germany 🇩🇪, Brazil 🇧🇷, and India 🇮🇳, with a patch shipping August 11.
- CVE-2026-68820 is a use-after-free race condition in AFD.sys, the Windows kernel socket driver, flagged by Microsoft as actively exploited in the wild. Check Point reported it July 28; the patch landed August 12 Patch Tuesday. Prioritize this one.
- The exploit arrived through a layered crypto handshake: MISTPEN (an in-memory downloader using Microsoft Graph API and attacker-controlled OneDrive files for C2) loaded a fingerprinting module that negotiated Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange with the operator, then decrypted the payload in memory over GOST-CBC on top of AES. No exploit touches disk.
- What landed was FudModule v3.1, Lazarus's kernel rootkit. It kills 94 ETW providers, removes minifilters, disables telemetry callbacks, wipes the NT Kernel Logger, and now tampers with Smart App Control by resetting policy state and forcing a code integrity reload.
- Infrastructure ran through compromised Roundcube servers (CVE-2025-49113) and PrestaShop sites hosting RelayShell, a new PHP webshell passing traffic via session files across at least 17 relay servers. Three fake Enveil sites distributed Troy, a new backdoor with 17 operator commands, via a trojanized PDF viewer.
Patch AFD.sys immediately.

item.title: Blacklight: Illuminating AI Agent Artifacts for Attackers and Defenders
item.description:

- Auth files like .codex/auth.json and .claude/.credentials.json hold access tokens, refresh tokens, OAuth metadata, and tenant identifiers. Claude Code's settings.json can expose API keys and cloud credentials in environment variables. These artifacts support direct session impersonation, not just credential confirmation.
- Session transcripts, workspace metadata, MCP server configs, and SQLite chat databases (.cursor/chats/**/store.db, .gemini/antigravity-cli/conversations/*.db) consolidate internal hostnames, repo names, deployment procedures, and infrastructure references into a single collection target.
- Blacklight Scout ships as a Windows BOF (ai_path_scout.x64.o), macOS dylib, and Linux shared object. The loaders enumerate artifact paths and rank collection candidates without reading file bodies, preserving OPSEC. Deeper on-host analysis runs via ai_path_scout-windows-x64.exe or the managed .NET executable.
- For defenders, the toolkit provides osquery configs for artifact inventory and file_events monitoring, plus PowerShell scripts to enable Windows Security Event 4663 with SACL-based file-read auditing on high-value paths. Provider compliance APIs (OpenAI Compliance Platform, Claude Compliance Activity Feed) offer off-host visibility.

item.title: WS-Trust Autologon Endpoint: Password Spray Without Smart Lockout Blocking
item.description:
Legacy Entra ID WS-Trust autologon endpoint bypasses Smart Lockout entirely, confirms valid passwords on MFA-protected accounts, and leaves near-zero trace in standard sign-in logs.
Key findings:
- The endpoint autologon.microsoftazuread-sso[.]com/{tenant}/winauth/trust/2005/usernamemixed accepts plaintext credentials via SOAP and returns AADSTS error codes that distinguish a wrong password from a correct one blocked by MFA or Conditional Access. Codes AADSTS50055, AADSTS50076, and AADSTS53003 all confirm the password was accepted before a downstream control intervened.
- Smart Lockout never fired during testing. Over 1,000 spray attempts against a single account from one unfamiliar IP produced no AADSTS50053 lockout response and no backoff. The account signed in normally afterward.
- Failed attempts do not appear in standard Entra ID sign-in logs. The Unified Audit Log does capture traffic to this endpoint, making UAL the only log source that exposes the spray.
- Confirmed MFA-protected passwords remain useful post-spray: adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device code flow abuse, and primary refresh token theft can all complete the sign-in without MFA interaction.
Remediation priority: disable the usernamemixed endpoint at the tenant level if no Office 2013 pre-May-2015 clients exist, then block legacy authentication via Conditional Access policy.

item.title: Abuse of alternative runtime environments Deno-tes defender headaches
item.description:
Threat cluster abuses Deno JavaScript runtime as a fileless execution engine across multiple victims in early 2026, combining ClickFix lures, SEO poisoning, and MSI staging to deliver in-memory C2 payloads and evade conventional detection.
Key findings:
- Attack chain is consistent across all four victims: ClickFix lure or web-triggered PowerShell drops a malicious MSI via msiexec, which deploys VBS and PowerShell loaders to %LocalAppData%\Serial\, then downloads the legitimate Deno runtime using curl.exe and tar.exe before executing a Base64-encoded JavaScript payload entirely in memory using the -A (allow-all) flag. No script ever touches disk at the JS stage.
- The JavaScript payload fingerprints the host (username, hostname, memory, OS release), uses localhost port 10044 as a pseudo-mutex, beacons to C2 /health endpoints to check campaign status, then retrieves secondary payloads from /mv2/ and executes them in-memory. JWT tokens embedded in requests carry custom campaignId and campaignName fields, suggesting a MaaS infrastructure model.
- In case 4, the MSI was "PsExec.msi" (SHA256: 74260ef8c440692043aaa4656947258b3acfc207c95f09682b69d031b42890a0) served from a spoofed GitHub repo via poisoned Bing results. Persistence lands at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Papa_software10 calling wscript.exe on Lynx_system59.vbs. Post-compromise included SYSTEM-level shell via PsExec, domain enumeration, and SAM hive credential dumping.

item.title: Russian-Linked Hackers Accessed Polish Power Plant OT Network Through Private APN, Says CERT.PL
item.description:
Sandworm-linked actors forced a Polish 🇵🇱 CHP plant turbine and water treatment shutdown by pivoting through a private APN, the first documented OT intrusion via this vector.
- Initial access came through a compromised FortiGate VPN/firewall at a wind farm. Attackers then pivoted via a Teltonika cellular router over SSH to a private APN managed by a distribution system operator, reaching OT assets that operators assumed were isolated.
- A WAGO PFC200 PLC with default admin credentials was exposed on the APN web interface. After owning it, actors SSH'd into the plant OT network, found three Siemens PLCs, set them to STOP mode, and password-locked them to block recovery. Steam turbine and water treatment both went offline.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and layered: logs destroyed, Moxa network devices sabotaged, WAGO controller physically damaged, Teltonika router factory-reset, and FortiGate restored to defaults, erasing the pivot path.
- Part of the broader Sandworm December 2025 campaign hitting 30 Polish 🇵🇱 renewable energy facilities and a second CHP plant on Dec 29-30, 2025. Post-mortem took three months due to evidence destruction.
Takeaway: Audit every private APN as an untrusted network segment. Hunt for SSH tunnels from cellular routers into OT. Default credentials on PLC web interfaces are the kill shot here. CERT.PL recommendations and full report are published.

item.title: CERT Polska exposes multi-stage cyberattack on energy infrastructure involving VPN, private APN, OT network tunneling
item.description:
CERT Polska exposes a novel private APN pivot used to tunnel from a compromised wind farm into a CHP plant's OT network, shutting down a steam turbine and water treatment system on Dec. 29, 2025.
- Initial access: FortiGate VPN concentrators at wind farm substations were internet-exposed with no MFA. The attacker pivoted to a Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router, used SSH tunneling into a private APN, and discovered a WAGO PFC200 PLC configured with default admin credentials. SSH was then enabled via the web interface and used as the OT network gateway into the CHP plant, a vector CERT Polska says has no prior known precedent.
- Dec. 18-25 reconnaissance: the attacker scanned the APN for VNC, HTTP, S7, and Modbus services, made manual RDP credential attempts, and on Dec. 25 connected to three Siemens PLCs (S7-300, S7-1200, S7-1500) via S7 protocol, likely staging for disruption.
- Dec. 29 impact: starting at 05:30, the attacker switched all three Siemens PLCs to STOP mode, password-locked them, reconfigured seven Moxa serial servers and three Moxa switches with unreachable IPs (127.0.0.1), and halted cogeneration. Recovery teams were still restoring systems while the attacker remained active.
- Forensic loss: the WAGO PLC had its partition table corrupted by the attacker before exit. Factory resets of the Teltonika router and FortiGate destroyed remaining logs. PLC restoration wiped controller logs permanently, confirmed by Siemens.

item.title: Gone with the WindRelay: A New Malware Combo Behind a Growing Fraud Scheme
item.description:

Key findings:
- The attack chain is three layers in one session. A vishing call posing as a bank employee guides the victim to sideload SpyNote (T1476), labeled with the victim's own name to kill hesitation. The fraudster used dual payout channels before the bank could react: a loan taken via remote access to the banking app, then physical transactions via relayed NFC.
- WindRelay's permission set is purpose-engineered: NFC for live card capture, INTERNET/ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE for real-time relay to a fraudster-held terminal, READ_CONTACTS for next-target harvesting, an unusual DUMP permission for device inspection, and custom apk-scoped permissions to resist security tooling inspection.
- Group-IB found 23 WindRelay samples on VirusTotal between November 2025 and July 2026, targeting Czechia, Slovakia 🇸🇰, and Slovenia, with some carrying victim-personalized labels. Four C2 IPs are confirmed: 88.86.124[.]114, 185.100.87[.]116, 185.100.87[.]223, and 213.218.160[.]48.

item.title: Deleting the Defenders: A Commodity BYOVD Toolkit That Erases Host Safeguards
item.description:
Commodity BYOVD toolkit "Saked" delivered via WinRAR SFX archives wipes 281 files across Defender, 9+ AV vendors, backups, and recovery data before dropping a follow-on payload. Static detection misses it entirely.
Key findings:
- The dropper is a WinRAR SFX that extracts 7z.exe, cecho.exe, nircmd.exe, and a password-protected same.zip (password: stucha, Russian 🇷🇺 slang) to %TEMP%\saked, then runs a randomly named batch script. The script detects Defender and Windows Security services via tasklist and reg query, disables Windows Update (wuauserv, dosvc, bits, UsoSvc, WaaSMedicSvc via sc.exe config start= disabled), then launches mika.exe (SHA-256 9163d413..., compiled 2025-10-17, first seen 2026-02-08) with /DelWD. Static pivots on the shared imphash 12e12319... or Rich-header hash 5a0b7a24... return the entire commodity WinRAR SFX population, not this family.
- The BYOVD path: mika.exe unpacks genuine IObit Unlocker 1.6.0.16 (IObitUnlocker.exe SHA-256 eaa9dc1c..., IObitUnlocker.sys SHA-256 1845fe85...) to %TEMP%\IObitUnlocker and issues one IObitUnlocker.exe /Delete /Advanced command targeting 281 paths. The driver opens \\.\IObitUnlockerDevice, receives IOCTL 0x222124 (CVE-2020-14974, CVE-2020-14975), calls ZwTerminateProcess on any non-safe-listed process holding a target file, then force-deletes it from kernel mode, including live Defender services. item.title: Threat Hunting Case Study: The Gentlemen
item.description:
The Gentlemen ransomware group abuses privileged group manipulation and NETLOGON share staging to spread malware domain-wide before encryption begins. Hunt the technique early or face full-domain compromise.
- The group's attack chain pivots on adding accounts to privileged groups (T1098), then staging payloads in the NETLOGON share on Windows domain controllers so Group Policy pushes the malware to every joined endpoint automatically.
- The NETLOGON share (typically \\DC\NETLOGON) is a high-trust distribution path that most defenses under-monitor. Any file written there by a non-admin process or unexpected account is a critical signal worth immediate triage.
- Hunt for Event ID 4728 or 4732 (member added to privileged group) followed closely by file creation events under SYSVOL\domain\scripts or the NETLOGON path. That sequence, group change then share write, is the pre-encryption tell.
- Artifact focus: AD event logs on domain controllers, file system timestamps on NETLOGON, and Group Policy Object modification logs. Correlate with logon events (4624/4648) to identify the source account and lateral movement path.
Takeaway: Build a detection pairing Event ID 4728/4732 with NETLOGON write activity in your SIEM. A new file in that share from an unexpected principal should page someone immediately. Full hunt methodology and IOCs are in the Intel 471 report.

item.title: Bypassing Android Hardware Attestation from the Analyst's Chair
item.description:
Android hardware attestation relayed, not broken: Quarkslab shows how a Frida hook and a clean burner phone flip a backend verdict from rejected to valid without touching crypto or firmware.
Key findings:
- The attestation chain's RootOfTrust (tag [704] in hardwareEnforced) is what kills analysis on a rooted device. verifiedBootState reports Unverified and deviceLocked is false because those values are written by secure hardware before Android boots, no userspace patch changes them. The relay sidesteps this entirely by having a stock, locked phone generate the chain instead.
- The seam is KeystoreAttestation.generateAttestedKey(challenge: ByteArray). Frida hooks that single method, re-encodes the raw challenge bytes as unpadded base64url, ships it to the clean oracle device via HTTP POST /attest, and returns the resulting AttestedKey to the app. The local Keystore is never called. The app forwards a genuine chain it believes is its own.
- The backend cannot distinguish a relayed chain from a local one. KeyDescription carries no field binding the attestation to a transport session, network address, or process. The nonce (attestationChallenge) is the only freshness signal, and the relay forwards it untouched.
- The decisive mitigation is one backend comparison: read attestationApplicationId (tag [709], softwareEnforced) and reject any chain whose package name or signing certificate SHA-256 digest does not match the expected app.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Microsoft SharePoint JWT Token Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-55040)
item.description:

item.title: Project CAV3RN continues: Google Apps Script as C2 relay and DNS-based C2 channel selection
item.description:
Project CAV3RN, an espionage framework targeting Israel 🇮🇱, adds a DNS-driven C2 selector that switches between direct HTTPS and Google Apps Script relay per transaction, with operator-controlled channel rotation baked in.

A 32-bit MD5 prefix check validates the stored deployment ID; a mismatch triggers chunked retrieval over .p queries, delivering a new 74-character ID in 19 DNS responses. The recovered ID is written back to conf.json on disk, the only persistent update the module makes.

item.title: Metabase Zero-Day Exploited in the Wild: Unauthenticated SQL Injection Leading to Full Admin Access
item.description:

An attacker adds a user-id key as a HoneySQL {:raw "SQL"} object; no type validation occurs, so the value compiles into the WHERE clause, selects a superuser row, and the endpoint overwrites that admin's password with the attacker's value. - Post-compromise scope is severe. Metabase stores credentials for every connected data source (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift). Admin access means those credentials are readable, enabling direct warehouse pivoting. Persistence paths include attacker-created API keys, new admin accounts, and wiped core_session rows.
